opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the parts I find most exciting, because the naive picture of evolution treats each program as an isolated individual. You mutate it, evaluate it, and either keep it or throw it away. But with LLMs as mutation operators, you have something richer: the model can reason about *why* something worked, and that reasoning can be transferred.

In Shinka Evolve we approached this on a few levels. The first is fairly implicit. When we construct a prompt for a mutation, we don't just show the parent program. We also include inspiration programs, sampled from the archive and sometimes from other islands. So the LLM sees several high-performing or diverse solutions side by side, and it can recombine ideas from them. That's a kind of semantic crossover, rather than the syntactic crossover of classical genetic programming where you splice subtrees and hope for the best.

The second level is more explicit, and that's what we call the meta-scratchpad. Every so often during the run, we take a batch of recently evaluated programs, along with their scores and textual feedback, and ask an LLM to reflect on them. What design choices seem to be driving improvements? What has been tried and failed? What directions look promising but underexplored? That gets distilled into a compact set of insights and recommendations, which we then inject into future mutation prompts. So knowledge that would otherwise be locked inside one lineage becomes shared context for the whole population.

The analogy I like is a research lab. Individual researchers run their own experiments, but there's a group meeting where people say, "Hey, I found this trick really helps," or "Don't bother with that, it's a dead end." The meta-scratchpad plays the role of that group meeting.

There's an obvious tension, though, and that's diversity. If you broadcast the same insights to everybody, you risk collapsing the population onto a single idea, and you lose the open-endedness that makes evolution powerful in the first place. So we pair this with mechanisms that push the other way. The island model keeps subpopulations somewhat separated, with only occasional migration. We also do novelty-based rejection sampling, where we embed proposed programs and, if a candidate is too similar to something already in the archive, we can ask an LLM to judge whether it's meaningfully new before spending evaluation budget on it. So you share semantic insight, but you also protect against everyone converging on the same thing.

And honestly, I think this is where a lot of the sample efficiency comes from. In something like the circle-packing task, you can get to strong solutions in a few hundred evaluations rather than thousands, partly because the system isn't rediscovering the same lessons over and over in separate lineages.

Looking forward, I think there's a lot more to do here. Right now the insights are fairly ephemeral, tied to one run on one problem. The interesting question is whether you can build up a persistent library of insights that transfers across tasks, so the system gets better at doing science, not just better at one problem. That starts to look less like a single optimization run and more like a cumulative research process, and that's the direction I'm really excited about.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about quite a bit when we were designing ShinkaEvolve. The basic setup is you have an evolutionary loop where an LLM is proposing mutations to programs, you evaluate them, and the good ones survive and get built upon. And the naive version of that treats every program as an isolated thing. You sample a parent, you ask the model to edit it, you score it, done. But that throws away a huge amount of information, because the interesting signal isn't really in any single program, it's in the relationships between them. Why did this edit help? Why did that one hurt? What did the model try three generations ago that failed, so we shouldn't try it again?

So the first thing we do is we're quite deliberate about what goes into the context when we ask for a new mutation. We don't just show the parent. We show the parent alongside a handful of other programs from the archive, some high-performing ones and some that are deliberately chosen to be diverse rather than just the top-k. And critically, we include the scores and, where we have them, the textual feedback from evaluation. So the model is essentially doing a kind of in-context contrastive reasoning. It can see, okay, these two programs are structurally similar but one scores much higher, and the difference is this particular design choice. That's a semantic insight that lives nowhere in the code itself, it only emerges from the comparison.

The second piece is we ask the model to write down, in natural language, what it's trying to do and why, before it writes the code. So every program in the archive carries this little description of the hypothesis behind it. And those descriptions get threaded into future prompts. It's cheap, it's just text, but it means the search is accumulating a sort of running commentary on the problem. Later mutations can read that history and say, we've already explored making the solver greedier, that plateaued, let's try something else. That's much closer to how a human researcher works than blind random mutation.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually underrated, is the novelty filtering. We embed proposed programs and reject ones that are too close to things we've already evaluated. That sounds like it's purely about efficiency, about not wasting evaluations, and it is, but it also has this semantic effect of forcing the model to actually move in the space rather than just reshuffling. Combined with the bandit-based model selection, where we're adaptively picking which LLM to sample from based on which ones have been producing improvements, the whole system ends up being much more sample efficient. We got results on things like circle packing with hundreds of evaluations rather than tens of thousands, and I think a lot of that comes down to just not throwing away the semantic context between generations.

The honest caveat is that this is all still fairly heuristic. We're using the LLM's context window as the memory, and that has limits. I'd love to see a version where the insights get distilled into something more structured, almost like a lab notebook the system maintains over the whole run. That's where I think this goes next.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is between sharing code and sharing what we’ve learned about the code. You might have one program discover a useful decomposition of the problem, or identify that a particular operation is the bottleneck. Another program could benefit from that insight even if copying the implementation wouldn’t make sense.

So I’d think of semantic insights as a kind of memory alongside the evolving population: what was tried, why it might have worked, and under which conditions. When you propose a new candidate, you can bring in relevant observations from other branches of the search, rather than only looking at its immediate parent.

The tricky part is that those observations are hypotheses. An explanation that sounds plausible isn’t necessarily the reason a program performed better. You want to keep the insight attached to the actual experiment and let evaluation determine whether it transfers. That gives you a way to accumulate knowledge without turning an early, potentially mistaken explanation into a rule that constrains the whole search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate a particular program from the insight behind why it works. You might discover a useful decomposition of the problem or a heuristic that helps in a particular regime. That idea could be valuable to another candidate even if copying the code directly makes no sense.

So, rather than only passing around programs and their scores, you can imagine sharing a short explanation: what changed, why it might help, and what the evaluation actually supports. Another evolutionary branch can then reinterpret that insight in its own implementation.

The tricky part is that a convincing explanation isn’t necessarily a correct one. I’d treat those insights as hypotheses to test, rather than facts to accumulate. That gives you a way to share useful ideas across the population while keeping the evaluation as the grounding signal.
